card.chief_complaint: sudden loss of consciousness during exertion

ask.changes_what: Positive: admit/monitor, ECG plus echocardiogram and cardiology review before discharge; negative: no change in workup.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not classify as non-exertional (reassuring) when timing is uncertain; treat ambiguous timing as exertional until echo/ECG are reviewed.
ask.escalation_warning: Exertional syncope with a murmur, family history of sudden death, chest pain, or abnormal ECG is a red flag for AS/HCM/VT: no discharge without cardiology evaluation.

evidence.citation: Berecki-Gisolf J, Sheldon A, Wieling W, et al. Identifying cardiac syncope based on clinical history: a literature-based model tested in four independent datasets. PLoS One. 2013;8(10):e75255.
evidence.location: Table 2, 'Syncope during effort' row (PMC3815402 full text)
evidence.population: Pooled derivation sample from 2 studies (Alboni 2001, Del Rosso 2008) reporting syncope during effort in adults with syncope
evidence.reference_standard: Final adjudicated cause of syncope in each primary study (cardiac vs non-cardiac)

evidence.citation: Del Rosso A, Alboni P, Brignole M, Menozzi C, Raviele A. Relation of clinical presentation of syncope to the age of patients. Am J Cardiol. 2005;96(10):1431-1435.
evidence.population: 261 consecutive patients aged >=65 y with unexplained syncope referred to secondary/tertiary hospitals (34% cardiac)
evidence.quote: Myoclonic movements, effort syncope, and supine position during loss of consciousness were the most specific (97%, 99%, and 99%, respectively) diagnostic criteria
evidence.reference_standard: Pre-specified ESC-based diagnostic criteria for cause of syncope

ask.how: Establish exactly when consciousness was lost relative to activity: during ongoing exertion (walking uphill, running, lifting) versus in the minutes after stopping. Ask what the patient was doing, whether there were palpitations or chest pain first, and whether a witness saw the collapse mid-activity.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of exertional syncope barely changes the probability of cardiac syncope (LR- ~0.9) because only ~13% of cardiac syncope is exertional.
ask.pitfalls: Collapse immediately after stopping exercise is typically reflex (post-exertional vasovagal) and must be distinguished from mid-exertion syncope; patients may not recall the exact timing. Exertional syncope is rare, so its absence is not reassuring.
ask.positive_finding: Syncope during exertion is uncommon but highly specific for a cardiac cause (pooled LR+ ~7; specificity 98-99%) and should prompt evaluation for aortic stenosis, HCM, ischemia, or ventricular arrhythmia before any return to activity.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or witness account; clarify timing precisely because post-exertional collapse is usually reflex.
ask.rationale: Syncope during exertion is a red flag for cardiac causes like aortic stenosis and mandates cardiac workup.
ask.title: Syncope during (not after) exertion

ask.changes_what: Typical prodrome + trigger, no heart disease, normal ECG: reflex syncope likely, limit testing. No prodrome, especially with heart disease or abnormal ECG: pursue cardiac evaluation/monitoring.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a reassuring prodrome to forgo ECG or to dismiss syncope in a patient with structural heart disease, exertional or supine syncope, or a family history of sudden death.
ask.escalation_warning: Syncope without prodrome plus heart disease, abnormal ECG, palpitations, exertional or supine occurrence warrants monitored cardiac evaluation.

evidence.citation: Berecki-Gisolf J, Sheldon A, Wieling W, et al. Identifying cardiac syncope based on clinical history: a literature-based model tested in four independent datasets. PLoS One. 2013;8(9):e75255.
evidence.population: Pooled derivation sample from published syncope cohorts: 424 cardiac vs 1552 non-cardiac syncope with nausea data
evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis of cardiac vs non-cardiac syncope in each source study

ask.how: Ask the patient (and any witness) what they felt in the seconds to minutes before losing consciousness: nausea, warmth, sweating, visual graying, feeling cold, headache; and what they were doing (standing long, micturition, cough, pain, after a meal). Ask about mood or behaviour change before and after the event and how long the warning lasted.
ask.negative_finding: Absent or very brief prodrome modestly raises the likelihood of cardiac syncope (LR about 1.7 in pooled derivation data) but is common in older patients with reflex syncope, so it does not rule cardiac causes in or out.
ask.pitfalls: Older adults with vasovagal syncope often report no prodrome and have amnesia for the event; prodrome duration and quality are poorly recalled without a witness. Arrhythmic syncope can be preceded by palpitations or brief lightheadedness that patients call a 'prodrome'.
ask.positive_finding: A typical autonomic prodrome with a situational trigger favours reflex (vasovagal/situational) syncope; individual prodromal features such as feeling cold, headache or mood change carry LRs of about 0.1-0.2 for cardiac syncope. A quantified history score (Calgary) diagnoses vasovagal syncope with sensitivity 89% and specificity 91%.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to recall the event; witness account improves accuracy.
ask.rationale: Absence of prodrome supports a cardiac or arrhythmic cause over reflex syncope, guiding urgency and monitoring.
ask.title: Prodrome before loss of consciousness (nausea, warmth, diaphoresis, visual graying) and situational trigger (micturition, cough, prolonged standing, pain, post-prandial) vs none

ask.changes_what: Positive: obtain ECG, telemetry and consider admission/monitoring for arrhythmia; negative: no change in cardiac-syncope probability.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of palpitations to de-escalate a syncope work-up in patients with structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, exertional or supine syncope.
ask.escalation_warning: Palpitations followed by syncope in a patient with known heart disease, family history of sudden death or an abnormal ECG warrants monitored observation and cardiology input.

evidence.citation: Berecki-Gisolf J, Sheldon A, Wieling W, et al. Identifying cardiac syncope based on clinical history: a literature-based model tested in four independent datasets. PLoS One. 2013;8(11):e75255.
evidence.location: Table 2 (Palpitations row), PMC3815402 open-access full text
evidence.population: Pooled derivation sample from 7 published syncope cohorts (Italy, Switzerland, Canada, USA); 468 cardiac and 1768 non-cardiac syncope patients with palpitation data
evidence.reference_standard: Final cause of syncope by each study's standardized diagnostic criteria (ESC-based work-up, EP study/tilt where used)
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac (arrhythmic or structural) syncope vs non-cardiac syncope

ask.how: Ask the patient (and any witness) whether they felt a racing, pounding or fluttering heartbeat in the seconds to minutes before losing consciousness, and whether it was rapid and regular or irregular. Distinguish it from the generic 'heart pounding' of a vasovagal prodrome that comes with warmth, nausea and sweating.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of palpitations does not exclude cardiac syncope; pooled literature LR for absence is about 1.0, so it changes little.
ask.pitfalls: In pooled derivation data palpitations were reported as often by non-cardiac (11%) as cardiac (8%) syncope patients, because vasovagal prodromes also include a pounding heart; the item behaves differently in patients with vs without heart disease (Alboni 2001).
ask.positive_finding: In the largest pooled literature sample (Berecki-Gisolf 2013; 468 cardiac vs 1768 non-cardiac syncope episodes) palpitations before syncope did not discriminate: LR+ 0.74, and the variable was excluded from the final model (p = 0.06). The EGSYS score nonetheless assigns palpitations +4 points, so a score-based workflow and this pooled estimate disagree. Treat palpitations as a prompt to characterise the episode (abrupt onset and offset, absence of autonomic prodrome, structural heart disease) rather than as independent evidence of arrhythmic syncope.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to recall the prodrome; corroborate with a witness where possible.
ask.rationale: Palpitations before syncope suggest arrhythmia, which would change monitoring and admission decisions.
ask.title: Palpitations immediately preceding syncope

examine.changes_what: Positive: obtain echocardiography and treat exertional symptoms as possible severe AS (avoid aggressive vasodilators/nitrates). Negative radiation: AS becomes an unlikely explanation.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm carotid pressure in patients with known carotid disease.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use murmur intensity or absence of a late peak to exclude severe low-flow/low-gradient AS in patients with reduced LV function; do not rely on auscultation alone when exertional syncope or heart failure is present.
examine.escalation_warning: Exertional syncope, angina or heart failure with a murmur suggestive of AS warrants urgent echocardiography and cardiology review; avoid nitrates, aggressive diuresis and vasodilators until AS severity is known.

evidence.citation: Bedside Physical Examination for the Diagnosis of Aortic Stenosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. CJC Open. 2024 (PMC10290951).
evidence.location: Discussion, paragraph on murmur characteristics (same paragraph: 'negative predictive value of its absence (LR = 0.2)')
evidence.population: Narrative aggregate of 4 small studies of patients with systolic murmurs (not bivariate meta-analysed)
evidence.quote: Data from a small sample from 4 studies revealed modest positive predictive value when this sign is present (LR of 3.7)
evidence.reference_standard: Echocardiography or left heart catheterization; AS of at least moderate severity

evidence.citation: Bedside Physical Examination for the Diagnosis of Aortic Stenosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. CJC Open. 2024 (PMC10290951).
evidence.population: 868 patients in 7 observational studies examined before echo or left heart catheterization (6 studies, 801 patients for S2)
evidence.target_condition: Aortic stenosis of at least moderate severity - component: diminished second heart sound

evidence.citation: Bedside Physical Examination for the Diagnosis of Aortic Stenosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. CJC Open. 2024 (PMC10290951).
evidence.population: 662 patients in 4 observational studies examined before echo or catheterization
evidence.target_condition: Aortic stenosis of at least moderate severity - component: systolic murmur radiating to the neck

evidence.citation: Etchells E, Glenns V, Shadowitz S, Bell C, Siu S. A bedside clinical prediction rule for detecting moderate or severe aortic stenosis. J Gen Intern Med. 1998;13(10):699-704.
evidence.population: 124 consecutive hospital inpatients referred for echocardiography, examined by a general internist and internal medicine resident
evidence.quote: Absence of a murmur over the right clavicle ruled out aortic stenosis (likelihood ratio [LR] 0.10; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.01, 0.44)
evidence.target_condition: Moderate or severe aortic stenosis (valve area <=1.2 cm2 or peak gradient >=25 mmHg) - component: absence of murmur over right clavicle

examine.how: With the diaphragm at the right 2nd intercostal space and along the left sternal border, time the murmur's peak against S1/S2 (or the carotid pulse); note whether the crescendo peaks in the second half of systole. Listen over both carotids and the right clavicle for radiation, and judge whether A2 is soft or inaudible at the base.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of any systolic murmur radiating to the neck or right clavicle makes moderate-or-severe AS unlikely (LR- about 0.05-0.11); an early-peaking soft murmur with a normal A2 favours sclerosis or flow murmur.
examine.pitfalls: Murmur loudness does not track severity (low-flow AS is soft), and HCM produces a similar harsh ejection murmur that peaks late but radiates poorly to the neck and has a preserved A2; most accuracy data come from cardiologist examiners in referral populations.
examine.positive_finding: A mid-to-late-peaking, harsh ejection murmur that radiates to the right carotid/clavicle with a diminished or absent A2 strongly raises the probability of moderate-or-greater aortic stenosis (LR+ roughly 8-100 for late peak; ~11 for soft S2).
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room, patient supine then sitting forward in held expiration; palpate the carotid simultaneously to time systole.
examine.rationale: A late-peaking systolic murmur radiating to the carotids is highly suggestive of severe aortic stenosis, which is a critical cause of exertional syncope.
examine.title: Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, late-peaking, radiating to carotids, with soft/absent A2

examine.changes_what: Positive: request echocardiography and manage as probable significant AS pending results. Negative: does not exclude AS; rely on murmur radiation and A2 to decide on echo.
examine.contraindications: Known carotid bruit or carotid disease, recent TIA/stroke, or carotid sinus hypersensitivity - palpate gently or omit.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use to exclude AS in elderly or hypertensive patients with stiff arteries, or to grade severity; do not palpate firmly in patients with carotid bruits or recent cerebrovascular events.
examine.escalation_warning: Delayed upstroke with exertional syncope, angina or heart failure suggests severe AS - urgent echocardiography, avoid vasodilators/nitrates and hypovolemia.

evidence.citation: Bedside Physical Examination for the Diagnosis of Aortic Stenosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. CJC Open. 2024 (PMC10290951).
evidence.population: 815 patients in 6 observational studies (mostly murmur/referral populations) examined before echo or left heart catheterization
evidence.target_condition: Aortic stenosis of at least moderate severity

examine.how: Palpate one carotid artery at a time with the fingertips below the angle of the jaw while auscultating the apex or watching S1; judge whether the pulse rises slowly and peaks late in systole (tardus) and whether its volume is small (parvus). Compare with your expectation for a brisk, sharp upstroke; check both sides sequentially.
examine.negative_finding: A normal brisk carotid upstroke only modestly lowers the probability (pooled LR- ~0.46, sensitivity ~57%); it does not exclude significant AS, especially in the elderly with stiff arteries.
examine.pitfalls: Arterial stiffness in the elderly and hypertension can normalize the upstroke despite severe AS, whereas a low-output state can produce a small pulse without AS; HCM typically gives a brisk, sometimes bisferiens, carotid pulse, which helps separate it from valvular AS.
examine.positive_finding: A slow-rising, low-volume carotid pulse substantially raises the probability of moderate-or-greater aortic stenosis (pooled LR+ ~9; RCE range 2.8-130).
examine.prerequisites: Patient supine or semi-recumbent and relaxed; never compress both carotids simultaneously.
examine.rationale: Delayed carotid upstroke further supports severe aortic stenosis and would prompt urgent echocardiography.
examine.title: Delayed and diminished carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus)

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant hypovolemia/bleeding or medication-related OH and act; negative: large blood loss unlikely, but moderate loss still possible.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is frankly hypotensive, has an unstable spine/pelvis, or cannot safely bear weight.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing measurements in a patient who is already hypotensive, too dizzy or weak to stand safely, or has an unstable spine or pelvis; a patient too dizzy to stand counts as a positive test.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive test in a patient with possible bleeding indicates large volume loss and should trigger resuscitation and source search, not observation.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.target_condition: Large acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.target_condition: Moderate acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy
evidence.quote: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent, even after up to 1150 mL of blood loss (sensitivity, 33%; 95% CI, 21%-47%, for supine hypotension)
evidence.target_condition: Blood loss up to 1150 mL - supine hypotension (comparator finding, not postural)

examine.how: Measure BP and pulse after >=2 min supine, then have the patient stand and repeat at 1 and 3 min (standing, not sitting). Record SBP fall >=20 or DBP fall >=10 mmHg, pulse rise >=30/min, and whether the patient is too dizzy to stand (count that as positive).
examine.negative_finding: A normal postural pulse response argues strongly against large blood loss (LR- about 0.03) but misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%). Normal orthostatics do not exclude hypovolemia from vomiting/diarrhea.
examine.pitfalls: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent even after 1 L blood loss. Beta-blockers blunt the pulse response; sitting instead of standing lowers sensitivity; mild postural dizziness alone has no proven value.
examine.positive_finding: A postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness is highly specific (98%) for blood loss and is nearly always present after large (>1 L) hemorrhage. In an older patient with syncope, an SBP fall >=20 mmHg reproducing symptoms supports orthostatic hypotension, though asymptomatic falls are common with age and medications.
examine.prerequisites: Automated or manual cuff, an assistant to steady the patient, supine rest of at least 2 minutes first.
examine.rationale: Orthostatic vitals help rule out orthostatic hypotension as a cause, which is important in the differential for syncope.
examine.title: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing
